title: Man Dies After Biting Explosive Handed to Him as Rasgulla Sweet
excerpt: Police in Madhya Pradesh's Dindori district say a 35-year-old man died after a crude boar-hunting explosive, described to him as a rasgulla, detonated in his mouth, and two men have been held as officers probe whether it was killing or mischief.
body:
• A 35-year-old man, identified by police as Rajendra Barautiya, died in Dindori district, Madhya Pradesh, after biting into a crude explosive described to him as a rasgulla.
  • Police say the device was a dough ball packed with gunpowder of a type used in some rural communities to kill wild boars, and it exploded in his mouth.
  • Two men have been held and a case registered for culpable homicide not amounting to murder, according to police accounts reported by CBS News and Daily Jagran.
  • Police say they have not yet established whether the act was intended to kill or was mischief, and the source of the explosive is under investigation.

A 35-year-old man has died in Madhya Pradesh after a crude bomb disguised as a traditional sweet exploded in his mouth, police said on Friday. The man was identified as Rajendra Barautiya, according to CBS News reporting of police accounts.

The incident took place in Dindori district in the central state of Madhya Pradesh. Daily Jagran reported that it happened at about 8 p.m. on Tuesday, November 10, in Padariya Chhanta village, after Barautiya had finished dinner and was sitting in the courtyard of his house in front of a fire. CBS News reported that he was gathered around a bonfire when a fellow villager brought the object and another man gave it to him.

What police say happened

Police identified the villager who handed Barautiya the object as Ramabhagat Barautiya. According to the accounts, he described it as a rasgulla, a soft, round sweet soaked in sugar syrup and traditionally eaten whole. Barautiya put it in his mouth and bit into it, and the device exploded.

"The bomb, used by some tribal people in the area to kill wild boars, was offered to this man. It exploded in his mouth."

— Rekha Singh, police officer, to AFP via CBS News

Barautiya was rushed to hospital with severe injuries but died. Daily Jagran reported that his family took him to Dindori District Hospital in an autorickshaw and that he died while undergoing treatment. His body was sent for a post-mortem examination on Wednesday and then handed over to his family, the report said.

The device and why it resembled a sweet

According to CBS News, some rural communities make the homemade devices by packing balls of dough with gunpowder, often sourced from firecrackers or quarries. The devices are designed to explode when an animal bites them, the report said, citing the Economic Times. Because the finished ball is round and pale, it can resemble a rasgulla.

That resemblance is central to the police account. On that account, this was a bait device passed off in conversation as food, not a genuine sweet bought from a shop. No source read for this article reported any contamination of shop-bought sweets, and readers should not draw that conclusion from this incident.

Arrests, charges and the open question of motive

Two men have been arrested and charged with culpable homicide not amounting to murder, CBS News reported. Daily Jagran gave a more detailed local account: Kotwali police station in-charge Durga Prasad Nagpure said police had detained Ram Bhagat along with another person, and that during questioning the accused allegedly claimed a boy had given him the explosive. The boy was also detained and was being questioned, the report said.

Daily Jagran reported that police registered a case under Section 105 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita and Sections 3 and 4 of the Explosive Substances Act. Investigators are probing how the accused obtained the bomb and whether personal enmity was behind the incident, the report said.

Police have not settled the motive. Officer Rekha Singh said, according to CBS News: "We don't know if the motive was to kill, or if it was a mischief. That is a matter of investigation." That distinction matters to the case that follows, and on the reporting available so far it remains open rather than decided.

What happens next

The next steps, on the sources read, are forensic and investigative rather than public-facing: establishing where the explosive came from, who handled it before it reached Barautiya, and what the men now held told investigators. The New Indian Express account cited by CBS News described shock and fear in the village after a casual evening conversation ended in a death, a reaction the local reporting also reflected.

For readers outside India, the essential facts are narrow. A man in one Madhya Pradesh village was handed a hunting explosive described as a sweet, bit into it and died. Police have held two men, registered a culpable homicide case, and said plainly that they do not yet know whether this was a killing or a prank that turned fatal.
nri_angle: A widely shared India news story with no direct action for diaspora readers; its relevance is the police investigation into crude hunting explosives circulating as ordinary food.
author: Diaspora Desk

items: Charges: Culpable homicide not amounting to murder
